identity.title: Fever onset temporally linked to a new drug (with rash/relative bradycardia)

technique.how: Chart every drug started or dose-changed in the preceding weeks (antibiotics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, heparin, and infusions) against the fever curve; note rash, eosinophilia, and whether the pulse is inappropriately slow for the temperature. Confirm by defervescence within about 72 h of stopping the suspect drug after infection is excluded.
technique.prerequisites: Medication administration record including PRNs; cultures and infection work-up already sent.
technique.contraindications: None; rechallenge is not recommended as a diagnostic step.

interpretation.positive_finding: Fever beginning after a new drug in a patient who looks well, with no source found and rapid defervescence on withdrawal, supports drug fever; rash or eosinophilia strengthens but is present in only a minority.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of rash, eosinophilia or relative bradycardia does not argue against drug fever; Mackowiak's series found these features infrequent and lag time highly variable.
interpretation.pitfalls: Textbook features (relative bradycardia, characteristic pattern, rash, eosinophilia) were uncommon in the systematic case series; drug fever remains a diagnosis of exclusion after infection, thrombosis and malignancy are considered.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: stop the most likely culprit and observe for defervescence within 72 h while continuing to exclude infection. Negative: keep hunting for a source.

sources.citation: Mackowiak PA, LeMaistre CF. Drug fever: a critical appraisal of conventional concepts. An analysis of 51 episodes in two Dallas hospitals and 97 episodes reported in the English literature. Ann Intern Med. 1987.
Cunha BA. The diagnostic significance of relative bradycardia in infectious disease. Clin Microbiol Infect. 2001.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute fever to a drug in a neutropenic, immunosuppressed, or hemodynamically unstable patient until infection is excluded.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Fever with rash plus mucosal involvement, facial edema, eosinophilia or organ dysfunction suggests DRESS/SJS - stop the drug immediately and escalate.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No reliability data; temporal attribution is a clinical judgment with no validated criteria found.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy estimate exists for temporal drug-fever attribution; status not_quantified. Mackowiak 1987 abstract (full text not in PMC) reports only qualitative findings: 'we found relative bradycardia in a minority of cases reviewed', 'a highly variable lag time', and 'an infrequent association with either rash or eosinophilia' (Abstract); no percentages are visible in the abstract, so none are recorded. Cunha 2001 (PubMed record has no abstract) is cited only as the narrative source for the relative-bradycardia concept; it provides no accuracy data. The 72-hour defervescence figure in technique/changes_what is conventional teaching (unverified recall).
